mappings.note: A badly crossed row: the stem holds a 'Tea from Assam' summary while the stored answers belong to a Coorg extract set. What the item actually assesses is extract comprehension (LO-1) plus two meaning questions (C-E1.1).
Parts i and ii retrieve the distinct traditions and the kuppia/kuffia resemblance (LO-1); later parts ask which description fits the extract and what the author's tone is, which is craft (C-E1.4).
Every part is answered from the supplied passage - the change in visitors and the list of sports. Retrieval, LO-1.
The -ing/-ed participial adjective drill (exciting vs excited, boring vs bored). The distinction is grammatical form, so C-E1.3 rather than vocabulary.
Write a paragraph about Coorg using those adjectives. The product is a piece of writing, C-E1.2, while the grammar drill it builds on is the separate C-E1.3 item.
Reads a passage on tea and then requires the learner to write their own account of it. Composition, C-E1.2.
What Pranjol ordered is a stated detail; retrieval, LO-1.
The groups of women plucking leaves are described in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Assam as the site of the largest concentration of plantations is stated; retrieval, LO-1.
'A sea of tea bushes' is the text's metaphor; recognising the comparison is a literary convention, C-E1.4, not plain retrieval.
What the two boys did on the journey is narrated; retrieval, LO-1, while the contrast in their attitudes is the LO-2 item.
Why one read while the other stared out asks for the difference between the two boys' situations and temperaments - character in context, LO-2.
'Elucidate your stance' on whether research spoils the thrill of discovery - an argued opinion, C-E1.2.
Write a paragraph giving two opinions from an article on India's diversity. Composition of the learner's own views, C-E1.2.
'Summarise your opinion on the given idea' of cultural assimilation - the learner's own position, C-E1.2.
The same contrast between the two boys' reactions, which turns on their different backgrounds. LO-2.
The Chinese emperor's accidental discovery is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
Rajvir's description of the Dhekiabari garden is given in the text; extraction, LO-1.
The differences (season, aprons, bamboo baskets) are all stated details to be gathered and set side by side; retrieval, LO-1.
What the two discussed on the train is narrated; retrieval, LO-1.
The Bodhidharma legend is told in the text; extraction, LO-1.
How the leaves are plucked and carried is described; retrieval, LO-1.
Both discovery legends are narrated in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Same pair of legends asked another way; retrieval, LO-1.
The landscape Rajvir sees is described in detail in the text; extraction, LO-1.
Assembles the facts the lesson gives about tea's history and cultivation; retrieval, LO-1.
First explains why Pranjol was unmoved (character in context, LO-2), then asks whether his reaction was appropriate, which is the learner's judgement (C-E1.2).
'State any one inference' about Rajvir from the extract - reading the character behind the detail, LO-2, rather than lifting a fact.
Draft an advertisement for a tea brand. Format, tone and persuasive style are what is marked, C-E1.2.
Lead part rules out a wrong gloss for 'buried his nose in his book' (C-E1.1); the rest retrieve the eighty-crore figure and the boys' situation from the extract (LO-1).
Part i names the figure of speech in 'a sea of bushes' (C-E1.4); parts ii and iii resolve 'doll-like figures' and a word choice, which is meaning (C-E1.1).
Part i explains Pranjol's indifference from his upbringing (LO-2); part ii unpacks what 'largest concentration of plantations' means (C-E1.1).
Authorship of 'A Baker from Goa' - knowledge about the work, C-E1.4, which no LO covers.
Authorship of 'Coorg'; recall about the work, C-E1.4.
Authorship of 'Tea from Assam'; recall about the work, C-E1.4.
'Pader' is named in the text; single-fact retrieval, LO-1.
Fill-in from the stated phrase 'friend, companion and guide'. Extraction, LO-1; the version that asks what it implies about him is the LO-2 item.
The bread-bangles the children wanted are named in the text; retrieval, LO-1.
Twice a day is a stated fact; retrieval, LO-1.
Fill-in naming the kabai as the baker's dress. Extraction, LO-1.
